blocks.text: Bryan Cantrill has a great line from a talk where he cautions against anthropomorphizing1 Oracle CEO Larry Ellison. I think it’s also a mistake to treat any tech company like a person. Here’s the full quote:

You need to think of Larry Ellison the way you think of a lawnmower. You don’t anthropomorphize your lawnmower, the lawnmower just mows the lawn, you stick your hand in there and it’ll chop it off, the end. You don’t think ‘oh, the lawnmower hates me’ — lawnmower doesn’t give a shit about you, lawnmower can’t hate you. Don’t anthropomorphize the lawnmower. Don’t fall into that trap about Oracle.
Companies are machines, not persons
Here are some examples of anthropomorphizing companies:
My company really owes me for that hard thing I did
I’m fighting the good fight against my company on issue X (e.g. accessibility) and they hate me for it
My company is vindictively retaliating against me because of that mistake I made
My company and I are partners in the mission to make the world a better place

All of these are mistakes. Your relationship to the tech company that employs you is not like a relationship with a person. It’s more like your relationship with your car2. If you drive poorly or fail to change your oil, your car may stop working or even kill you, but it doesn’t love or hate you. It has no sense of fairness. It’s simply a dangerous, useful machine: useful enough to be worth getting into despite the risks. Anthropomorphizing it makes it harder to avoid those risks3.

Why is it so hard to avoid this trap? First, humans anthropomorphize everything by default. Second, whenever you’re interacting with the company, you’re interacting with a person: your manager, your colleague, someone in HR, and so on. Third, when you’re in the power of some entity, it’s psychologically comforting to think of it like another human. This is the same principle that caused early humans to attribute lightning to the power of Zeus, because Zeus (unlike electrical imbalances in storm clouds) can be placated with prayer and sacrifice.
Disproportionate efforts and rewards

Relationships with machines are very different from relationships with people. The biggest difference is that machines do not respect effort. If you put a lot of work into doing a favor for a friend, your friend will appreciate it even if the favor itself is not a big deal. Conversely, if you help somebody out at trivial cost to yourself, that help will be relatively unappreciated. But a car doesn’t care how much effort you put into maintaining it. If you spend hours replacing a car’s engine, but the brake line is damaged, the car won’t remain functional out of respect for your effort on the engine: instead, the brakes will fail, killing you.

Tech companies work like this. Everyone who’s worked at one for long enough knows that it’s very hard to predict what work will be high-impact. The project you slaved over for months will often get a “nice, now what’s next” reaction, while the tool you built in fifteen minutes (or the question you answered in a Slack channel) will sometimes get wild praise and recognition. This can drive engineers a little mad, because they’re anthropomorphizing their tech company, and a person who behaved like this would be dangerously unstable. But if you treat your company like a machine, this shouldn’t be surprising at all.

It’s hard to predict high-impact work, but it’s not impossible. The best way to operate at a big tech company — as I’ve said again and again — is to try and develop this skill, and to spend most of your time looking for the low-effort high-reward wins. It’s hard to do that if you’re secretly imagining your company as a person.
Anthropomorphism is a dangerous shorthand

A natural objection here is to point out that tech companies (unlike cars) are composed of people who might indeed owe you, hate you, love you, and so on. According to this view, when people say “my company hates me”, they aren’t making the mistake of anthropomorphizing a corporation, they’re using shorthand to say “my boss and skip-level hate me”. I think this is still a dangerously sloppy way to think.

In my experience, engineers who think they’re hated are often not. Managers in large tech companies do hold grudges, but (particularly the higher up you get) are tolerably cold-blooded. You don’t get to senior director or VP by needlessly throwing away useful tools. I can recall a few cases4 where engineers told me they were hated, but I later found out5 that managers considered them dangerous or unreliable: loose cannons whose usefulness didn’t outweigh their tendency to go off the rails and cause damage. From the perspective of the engineer being forced out of the company, it feels like you’re being run out of town by people who hate you. But if you want to avoid being run out of town, it’s useful to recognize when you’re being treated as a defective tool.

It’s also useful to keep in mind the difference between “my manager hates me” and “my company hates me”, because managers are often temporary. You can sometimes just wait out a bad relationship with your manager. You’ll have a slightly uphill battle with the next one — since the handoff won’t be positive — but it’s certainly possible to get back on track. If you can figure out why your manager hates you, you might also be able to fix it (or at least mitigate6 it).
Don’t go too far in the other direction

Engineers who’ve learned not to anthropomorphize tech companies sometimes go too far in the other direction, by treating companies as a computer program. This is the wrong kind of machine: tech companies aren’t people, but they aren’t programs either. They operate on incentives and illegible interpersonal relationships, not on consistent logical steps.

The classic example of this is the engineer who reads the company handbook cover-to-cover and makes sure they follow all the rules. When they’re looking to be promoted, they take the role guidelines and make sure they’re following them point-by-point. They take what they’re told very literally: when the company says “X is our top priority”, they internalize that.

The problem with this is that handbooks, guidelines and internal communications are the legible superstructure of a massive illegible web of dependencies that make up the actual operations of any company. That superstructure will not cover the real criteria for promotions, or the rules that are designed to be broken. The “top priority” of the superstructure can rapidly shift, leaving literal-minded engineers confused and disheartened.
Conclusion

It’s understandable to feel ill-treated by a company, or to harbor resentment — particularly since there are actual humans at the company who are involved in that treatment of you. But companies themselves don’t hold grudges, even as they force out people who they’re incentivized to force out7. It can even be a mistake to anthropomorphize very senior managers, whose work personas are more identified with the machine the higher up you go8. I suppose at the top you have Larry Ellison, as Bryan Cantrill says, who is better modeled as a lawnmower than as a human being.

No relationship with an individual person at your company will save you from being careless with the machine: it will chew you up and spit you out. You need to learn how to drive the car. This is scary, because it means that sometimes you will just get punished for no reason. But it’s also good news, because it means that you can get disproportionate rewards for relatively little effort, so long as you make the right decisions.

Treating as a human.
↩

I like this example better than Cantrill’s lawnmower because cars are more central to our lives, like jobs are, and are also far more dangerous.
↩

For instance, if you’re prone to thinking “my car loves me, it wouldn’t spin out when I take this hard turn on gravel”, you are more likely to crash.
↩

Though certainly not all. Grudges do exist.
↩

Of course, this is my interpretation of the situation, and could be wrong.
↩

There are a range of techniques here, ranging from “do all your paperwork defensively” to “find some out-of-the-way project” to “ingratiate yourself with your skip-level”.
↩

For instance, people who make their managers look bad, or who publicly point out the inevitable inaccuracies in legible reports, or who campaign against the current big push the company is making.
↩

I say “work personas” because these people often have a rich personal life that is largely firewalled off from their work selves. For more on how managers come to identify with the rules of the organization, I recommend Robert Jackall’s Moral Mazes, a book that has informed much of my thinking and that I will some day write a long-form review of.

blocks.text:
Portrait mode launched 10 years ago today. 

I think it resonated with people because it didn’t feel digital. It felt analog. And this was likely because the inspiration behind its technique went all the way back to oil painting. Sometimes pure math isn’t enough; you need to combine it with insights from the liberal arts. 

If you recall Portrait mode shipped a month after the iPhone did. This was because this insight about oil painting took a while to figure out. 

Initially, Portrait mode was seen as a giant math problem. You’d do disparity calculations on the two sensors and output a depth map. The problem was this approach feels and looks digital; it feels fake. In areas without texture, it’s impossible to do this calculation. In areas with ultra fine detail, a lower resolution depth map leads to terrible transitions and a full resolution depth map takes forever to compute. One solution would be to reduce the amount of bokeh so the issues are not as obvious. But then you lose the whole point of the feature, which was to make it look like you had a large, wide-open lens.

The solution to this conundrum—the tradeoff between artifacts and the amount of blur— was quite elegant, but it took a while to stumble across. There’s a saying in painting that if you get the eyes right, nothing else matters. Inspired by this principle from oil painting, the idea was to make sure we never got the eyes wrong. We brought in a machine learning block to find the eyes, and draw a mask layer that protected them, then paired that with the disparity depth map. Counterintuitively, the solution was not to decrease the amount of blur, it was to increase it. The additional blur that we could add once the eyes were protected allowed us to hide the artifacts that were create by bad depth calculation. We let the ears go soft, let the nose go a bit soft. This is that wide open look that people loved, even if people didn’t realize that the ears going soft was why.

I was thinking about this recently with regard to AI. We’ll be able to do more amazing things… we just need to study the masters who came before us.

blocks.text: Jay Peters
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale today, but a few units already have broken screens. According to posts on Reddit about the affected units, the issue appears to be happening at a similar spot on all of them: Some kind of problem shows up on the inner screen along the hinge and a strange bright line (or lines) across the right side of the display.
Here’s how one user in Australia described what happened to their phone:

Had my iPhone Duo for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen.As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.There were no marks or damage on the inner screen’s surface or the external hinge to suggest anything had been caught or damaged.
The user said that the Apple Store replaced their phone with “a brand-new one on the spot.”
A post showing an image of another broken screen includes a video in a comment demonstrating yet another.
And a separate Reddit thread collected other pictures of affected Duos.
Apple didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

articles.title: Gadget Review: LiberNovo Omni - the USB-C powered office chair ★★★★⯪
articles.titleZh: Gadget Review: LiberNovo Omni - the USB-C powered office chair ★★★★⯪
articles.summary: Gadget Review: LiberNovo Omni - the USB-C powered office chair ★★★★⯪

blocks.text: Whenever a company asks me to review their gadgets, I always ask if it is USB-C powered. If not, I'm not interested. So, welcome to the future where your chair is USC-C rechargeable!
WHAT?!
The LiberNovo Omni looks like a standard office chair - but has two secret features.
First, is that it is exceedingly comfortable. Full foam cushions, lovely headrest, and a recline which almost gets you horizontal.
Second, it is USB-C powered. There's a small battery pack which plugs in to the chair. Why? Read on!
OK, let's start at the beginning.
Assembly

Flat-pack chairs like this are normally notoriously hard to assemble. The LiberNovo bucks that trend - not only does it include a how-to video, it prints the instructions on a MASSIVE piece of cardboard.
I'm used to peering at tiny black-and-white diagrams in a flimsy paper booklet. IKEA could learn a thing or two from this.
The screws are all labelled and a hex-driver is included. What's an even nicer touch, however, is some safety gloves:
That's the sort of thing which doesn't cost much to the manufacturer, but is such a thoughtful gesture. There's nothing too sharp as you assemble, but who wants to cover their new chair in blood, eh?
The parts come in two large boxes, but there aren't that many separate bits.
Building it took about half an hour. It's easier with a friend to help - as are most things in life - but doesn't require much skill.
Go Back To The USB-C Part Again Please?
The battery pack is a 2200mAh unit with a USB-C port to recharge. It connects in to the chair with this slightly unusual connector:
The internals of the chair have a USB-C cable to connect everything up.
LOL!
YES BUT WHY DOES A CHAIR NEED A BATTERY PACK??!?!
On the side of the left arm-rest are three buttons.
Two of them move the lumbar-support up and down. Depending on how your back is feeling and how far you are reclined, you can adjust the the back-support position.
And the 3rd button?
That's the build-in back massager, silly!
Is that useful?
Yes. Being able to instantly adjust the back support without having to twist around is fantastic, especially for those of us reaching a certain age.

The "massage" feature essentially just moves the support up and down for five minutes before returning to its previous location. When sat upright, it feels great. But the real benefit is when you're laying down.
How flat does this thing go?

160° - not quite flat, but good enough when you're taking a break from Typing Real Hard. You don't want a photo of me sprawled out, so LiberNovo have helpfully provided some stock photos of much better looking folk.
It is incredibly stable. At no point did it tip over or feel like it was going to deposit me on the floor. What really helps is the included foot stall.
No Feets On Seats
Unsurprisingly, this is not USB-C powered. A sturdy plastic footrest with a deeply padded leg rest on top.
Again, assembly was a cinch - follow the large printed instructions and clip it together. It's rated for 40㎏, so you shouldn't stand on it but it is more than enough to rest your weary legs.
Price
I hope you're sitting down for this.

Direct from LiberNovo, you can expect to pay around £700 - although there are bundles with extra batteries, the footrest, and even an eye mask which will shoot that price up. You can get the full bundle on Amazon for around £1,000.
There's two ways to look at that price. Firstly, youch. But, alternatively, that's still cheaper than a Herman Miller Aeron. And Herm's doesn't come with a built-in lumbar massage.
(There is also an upgraded version which has a built in fan under the seat. Personally, I suggest eating a healthier diet.)
I can't deny that's a chunk of change. If you're anything like me, you probably spend most of your day sat down. You might as well sit on something comfortable.
Final Thoughts

Having the back-rest adjustable via arm-rest buttons is a genius touch. I just wish it went further. I'd love a control panel (or, dare I say it, app) which let me adjust the seat height, recline, headrest position etc. Who can be bothered with fiddly manual levers when electricity can do the work for us?
Building this chair was a breeze - and it was delightful to get a pair of safety gloves with it.

The chair is extraordinarily comfortable and the back massage, while not on the level of a "shiatsu" style heated massage pillow, is delightfully pleasant. Would I lie all the way back and sleep in it? Yeah! Certainly more comfortable than an economy airline seat.

If you spend a lot of time sitting at your computer, your arse deserves something supportive. Your back deserves some love too. Yes, the USB-C power-pack is a little bit of a gimmick - but it is a hell of a good one.
In my opinion, this is worth splashing out on.

articles.title: Computing polar triangles with linear algebra
articles.titleZh: Computing polar triangles with linear algebra
articles.summary: Computing polar triangles with linear algebra

fullText.siteName: John D. Cook | Applied Mathematics Consulting

blocks.text: The previous post defined the polar triangle of a spherical triangle in terms of its sides and angles, but it doesn’t construct the triangle. It only specifies one of a family of triangles located anywhere on the sphere.

How do we know that polar triangles exist? There is a geometric construction that starts with a spherical triangle and constructs a unique new spherical triangle, and one can show that this new triangle has the angles and sides described in the previous post.

There is also a linear algebraic construction of polar triangles, and that’s the topic of this post. In a nutshell, take your sphere to be the unit sphere in 3D. Write the coordinates of each vertex as the columns of a matrix. Invert that matrix and normalize each row. Then the rows are the coordinates of the polar vertices.
This process is an involution: the polar of the polar of a triangle is the original triangle.

The following Python code illustrates the process described above. It begins with a triangle on the globe with vertices A, B, and C at Chicago, Quito, and Paris respectively. It computes the polar triangle, then computes the polar of that, and shows that the result is the original triangle.

import numpy as np

def latlon_to_cartesian(lat_deg, lon_deg):
    lat = np.radians(lat_deg)
    lon = np.radians(lon_deg)
    x = np.cos(lat) * np.cos(lon)
    y = np.cos(lat) * np.sin(lon)
    z = np.sin(lat)

How do we know that polar triangles exist? There is a geometric construction that starts with a spherical triangle and constructs a unique new spherical triangle, and one can show that this new triangle has the angles and sides described in the previous post.

There is also a linear algebraic construction of polar triangles, and that’s the topic of this post. In a nutshell, take your sphere to be the unit sphere in 3D. blocks.text: I’ve written before about the law of cosines on a sphere:
cos(c) = cos(a) cos(b) + sin(a) sin(b) cos(C).

But that’s just one of two laws of cosines on a sphere. The equation above is the law of cosines for sides. The law of cosines for angles is typographically very similar, just inverting the case of the letters used as arguments.
cos(C) = cos(A) cos(B) + sin(A) sin(B) cos(c).

Incidentally, the law of cosines for sides shows how the sides of a spherical triangle determine the angles. The law of cosines for angles shows how, unlike in the case of plane geometry, angles determine the sides.
Two kinds of angles

Let’s back up and say what the letters refer to. As is conventional in plane geometry, the sides of a triangle are a, b, and c, and the angles are A, B, and C, with a being the side opposite the angle A, and similarly for the other letters.
However, unlike plane geometry, the sides are also angles, but of a different sort. The sides a, b, and c are central angles, and the “angles” A, B, and C are dihedral angles.

The sides are arcs of a great circle. The side a, for example, is a portion of a great circle, running between the vertices at B and C [1]. Think of a plane that contains the center of the sphere O and the vertices B and C. The length of a is the angle at O.

The angles A, B, and C are the angles at which great circles meet. In the formalism of differential geometry, these angles exist in the tangent plane at the vertices. These angles are intrinsic, measured along the (tangent plane of) the surface of the sphere. The central angles are extrinsic, measured in a plane that cuts through the sphere to its center.
Polar triangles

Now because sides are angles and vertices are angles, we can interchange the two kinds of angles to form the polar triangle of the original triangle. This is a new triangle whose central angles are the complements of the original dihedral angles, and whose dihedral angles are the complements of the original central angles. In symbols,

a′ = π − A
b′ = π − B
c′ = π − C
A′ = π − a
B′ = π − b
C′ = π − c

Now we return to the laws of cosines at the top of the post: the law of cosines for angles is the law of cosines for sides applied to the polar triangle. Every equation in spherical trigonometry has a polar counterpart.

[1] There’s some overloaded terminology here, just as in plane geometry. The symbol a is used to denote a side of a triangle and also the length of that side. The symbol A is used to denote both a vertex and the dihedral angle at that vertex.

articles.title: How much you can make in an entry level cyber security job
articles.titleZh: How much you can make in an entry level cyber security job
articles.summary: How much you can make in an entry level cyber security job

blocks.text: How much you can make in an entry level cyber security job is a good question. We’ve all heard there is a shortage of people in cyber security, and while the money is good, there are certain limits. In this blog post, I’ll talk about the limits of the entry level cyber security job, and some possible career paths.
The entry level six figure job. Or not.

You will sometimes hear that cyber security jobs make six figures. And I don’t want to pour cold water on your hopes and dreams, but the entry level cyber security jobs typically do not. And when they do, it’s in places that have a high cost of living. If you make $100,000 in New York City, that’s the same as making $41,000 in Omaha.

I saw a LinkedIn post suggesting that people have this expectation, and it’s also something I have experienced first hand. I don’t want to give too much detail, but I once had a co-worker who finished a degree in cybersecurity and she let her displeasure be known that she wasn’t making $100,000. The problem with that was, at the time, no one but her manager was making $100,000 either.

I don’t like talking specifics about salary, and your mileage will certainly vary. I can point to a specific time when I crossed that threshold. In my case, I had a former employer and a prospective future employer who were both interested in me, because I could solve a specific problem for them. I told one about what the other was thinking in terms of salary, because I wasn’t sure both of them were on the same page. Both of them were on the same page.
Which job did I take?

But I didn’t just take the job that offered more money. One of the jobs had little or no advancement opportunity. The money was good, but that was as high as I was going to go with that organization, and the chances of using that to make anything other than a lateral move weren’t all that good. The other job, besides the money, offered valuable experience that built on experience I already had, but also offered new experience, and also positioned me to greatly expand my network.
But I’m getting ahead of myself a little bit. Let’s talk about how to get to that point.
What they don’t teach you in school about cyber security

Years ago, there was a best-selling book titled What They Don’t Teach You at Harvard Business School. The point of the book was that while there are valuable things you learn in the classroom, to be really valuable, you need to know things that you won’t learn in the classroom. It also pairs up with the book What They Teach You at Harvard Business School to make a great meme.

If you want to be worth $100,000, you need to know things that people graduating in a few months don’t know. Or at the very least, you need to be doing those things in production environments, not in lab settings.

In my case, what pushed me over that threshold was I reached a level of experience where I could solve a very specific problem for either of those two prospective employers. I could offer both of them something other than general knowledge. It was specific knowledge and experience that pushed me over the threshold.
Other companies who just wanted to utilize the general knowledge I had didn’t value me as highly.
Gaining the knowledge that makes you worth $100K

So to do that, you need to get your first job. Even if the pay isn’t very good. And even if it’s not strictly a security job. One of the best things you can do is take enough classes in general IT that you can get a job in IT rather than in security.

My career path is a bit unusual. But most of the ways I’m able to provide value leverage my operational system administrator experience. I can tell another security person when a system administrator isn’t being straight with them. I know their language, and I know the playbook.

And just this past week I had a conversation with a member of the technical support team at work. He knew what our employer says about running its products on VMware. But I was able to tell him when you can break that rule and under what specific circumstances. He understood it after I explained it to him. But since he didn’t have VMware experience, he needed someone to tell him.
Short term pay hit, but long term gain

So I think it’s worth it to take a job as a system administrator for a few years, even if it means taking a pay hit. And if you can’t find a job as a system administrator, there are opportunities in desktop support.

And then, whatever role you find yourself in, volunteer for security related tasks. For example, when I was a system administrator, nobody wanted anything to do with antivirus. I ended up doing antivirus and event log collection and patching because nobody else wanted to do them. It took me 7 years to accumulate 5 years of security experience, which sounds like a rip off, but look at it another way. My first security job wasn’t an entry level security job. I was able to apply for a job that needed 5 years of security experience, and I landed it. And after getting CISSP and about five years of experience in full-time security roles, I was ready to jump another pay grade.

And that’s good news. The shortage for security professionals is at the mid and senior levels, not so much the entry level. You can get a job as a SOC analyst and make decent money, and the experience is good. But you’ll be up against a huge number of applicants. Perhaps as many as 3,000. There won’t be as many applicants for those sysadmin and desktop support jobs.
What to say in your interview

And when they ask you in the interview, simply say you took security classes because of interests you, but you’re a technologist. You like technology, you like the city of the job is in, and you like the company. Make sure you know enough about the city and the company to be able to back that up. You can also say that it and security frequently have to work together, so having a background in security will make you a more effective IT professional.

And once you get in, interact with the security team as much as you can. If the company has a security champions program, participate in that. If there is an initiative to roll out security tools, participate in that. Examples of that include deploying Crowdstrike or Splunk or Nessus agents. If the security team needs help from the IT team in managing any on-premise tools, or setting up things like single sign on or multifactor authentication, volunteer for that. It all counts as security experience.
Finding opportunities

A good way to find opportunities is to watch job listings. I’m not saying to go get a new job right after you just got one. But look at jobs that are out there, and find something that sounds good to you, but is out of your reach. Look at the experience it requires, and look for opportunities to get some time with those tools or a competing tool. Use those job listings to figure out where you want to be, and how to get there from where you are at the time.
Keep watching, and keep making adjustments along the way.
Making the pivot into a cyber security job

And then, when you are ready to make your move, tailor your resume for that job. You will have 3 to 5 years of experience with your first full-time employer, plus your education, plus any internships or part-time jobs you had. Take the job duties for the job that you want and relate them to what you did at your first full-time job, and if possible, at your part-time jobs or your internships. And when it comes to your education, mention specific classes that apply to those job duties.
If your resume lands on my desk, you want me to read that resume and conclude that you have been working toward this position for seven or eight years.

And when you get into the interview, as long as you have enough experience that you can talk intelligently about all of the things that you list, you’ll pull it off. Maybe not the first time, but the thing about job searches is whether you interview with one company or 10, you can only accept one job offer. As long as you get one decent offer, it doesn’t matter if it’s the first or the 10th company extending it.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
